label: When Someone Won't Change
framing: You cannot repent for another person, no matter how much you love them, and some of the hardest grief is loving someone who will not turn. Scripture is honest that even God grieves the unrepentant heart he will not force, and it teaches you to keep loving while you stop trying to play the role only God can fill.
cultural: The biblical world had no illusion that influence equals control, watching kings and prophets and parents pour themselves out on people who would not listen. The whole prophetic tradition is the record of a faithful love that kept calling even when no one came, a God who pleads but does not coerce, because forced change is not change at all.
historical: The father of the prodigal, in Jesus' parable, did not chase his son into the far country or drag him home; he let him go and watched the road. From Jeremiah weeping over a people who would not turn around 600 BC to pastors today sitting with families worn down by a loved one's addiction, the church has learned the hard wisdom of loving without controlling, releasing without abandoning.
application: Make peace with what you cannot change, and pour your effort into what you can, your own response, your own boundaries, your own walk with God. Stop the rescuing that lets the pattern continue, since enabling is not love. Keep the door open and the prayer going. And entrust the person to the only One who can reach the will you cannot, which is most of the grief and all of the hope.

verses.text: Jesus looked at him, loved him, and said to him, “There is one thing you lack: Go, sell everything you own and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow Me.” But the man was saddened by these words and went away in sorrow, because he had great wealth.
verses.where: Jesus looks at the rich man, loves him, and names the one thing he lacks, and the man goes away grieving, because he had great wealth. The site's note says it is the only call to follow Jesus in Mark that is refused, and that Mark does not say what became of him. Jesus loved him and let him go; he did not chase him down the road or lower the call.

verses.text: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!
verses.where: At the end of his woes, Jesus laments over Jerusalem: how often he longed to gather her children as a hen gathers her chicks, and they were unwilling. The site's plain note says these words were spoken by a Jew who loved Jerusalem and wept over it, and that his last word was not I am done with you but how often I have longed. Jesus knew what it was to love people who would not come.

verses.text: How could I give you up, O Ephraim? How could I surrender you, O Israel? How could I make you like Admah? How could I treat you like Zeboiim? My heart is turned within Me; My compassion is stirred!
verses.where: God remembers how he loved Israel, called it out of Egypt and taught it to walk, and how the more he called the farther it ran. Then, as the site's note says, his own heart recoils from destroying Ephraim completely: how could I give you up? Scripture lets us hear the grief of God over people who keep turning away, and it is not a cold grief.

verses.text: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, “What do you people mean by quoting this proverb about the land of Israel: ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge’? As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, you will no longer quote this proverb in Israel. Behold, every soul belongs to Me; both father and son are Mine. The soul who sins is the one who will die.
verses.where: The exiles were repeating a proverb that blamed their suffering on their parents' sins, and God forbids it: every life belongs to him, and, as the site's note says, each person will live or die by his own ways. The chapter puts responsibility where it belongs. A parent, a spouse or a friend is not the cause of another adult's refusal to turn, and cannot turn for them.

verses.text: Cast away from yourselves all the transgressions you have committed, and fashion for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit. Why should you die, O house of Israel? For I take no pleasure in anyone’s death, declares the Lord GOD. So repent and live!
verses.where: The same chapter ends in a plea: God takes no pleasure in anyone's death, so turn and live. The site's note gathers the whole chapter into that plea. God's patience with someone who will not change is not indifference; he wants them to live.

verses.text: The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance.
verses.where: Answering scoffers who said nothing ever changes, Peter says the Lord is not slow but patient, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance. The site's note sets this in his answer to those who mocked the waiting. What looks like God doing nothing may be God waiting, and his waiting is mercy.

verses.text: ‘Sir,’ the man replied, ‘leave it alone again this year, until I dig around it and fertilize it. If it bears fruit next year, fine. But if not, you can cut it down.’”
verses.where: In the parable of the barren fig tree, the vinedresser asks for one more year, promising to dig around it and fertilize it. The site's note says the parable ends there and the reader never learns what the tree did, and the plain note says mercy that gives time also does real work to help the tree grow. Patience in Scripture is active, and it is not endless indifference to fruit.

verses.text: Watch yourselves. If your brother sins, rebuke him; and if he repents, forgive him.
verses.where: Jesus sets out an order: when a brother sins, rebuke him, and when he repents, forgive him. The site's plain note says forgiveness names the wrong and then refuses to hold it over the other person, that it is not the same as trusting someone again, and that a person who says I repent again and again for the same harm, and keeps doing it, has not turned at all. Words alone do not make it safe to stay.

verses.text: As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly.
verses.where: Proverbs uses a hard picture for the fool who returns to his folly, a dog returning to its vomit. The site's note on the chapter calls it one of three portraits, the fool, the slacker and the meddler. Wisdom does not pretend a repeated pattern is a new beginning, and it does not stake everything on the next promise.

verses.text: Now the LORD said to Samuel, “How long are you going to mourn for Saul, since I have rejected him as king over Israel? Fill your horn with oil and go. I am sending you to Jesse of Bethlehem, for I have selected from his sons a king for Myself.”
verses.where: God asks Samuel how long he will go on mourning for Saul, and sends him to Bethlehem. The site's note says God sends the grieving Samuel to anoint one of Jesse's sons. The grief for someone who would not change was real, and God did not scold it; but he did not let it be the end of Samuel's obedience either.

misread.taken: Love bears all things, hopes all things, endures all things is used to tell someone that real love never stops waiting for another person to change, and must keep enduring whatever they do, however long it lasts.
misread.says: The site's plain note on the passage says plainly that Paul is describing love that does not hold grudges or seek revenge in ordinary life together, not telling anyone to hide abuse, keep quiet about harm, or stay where they are in danger. In the same breath Paul says love takes no pleasure in evil but rejoices in the truth. Keeping a record of what someone has done, for safety or to get help or justice, is not a failure of love. Hope can go on for a person while the door is closed to the harm they do.
misread.text: It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

whole: If the person who will not change is hurting you, threatening you or putting your children in danger, your safety and theirs come first: tell someone you trust and get help, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Waiting for someone to change is not a reason to stay in harm's way. Many people carry a quieter version of this grief. A husband who promises to stop drinking every Monday. A grown son who keeps asking for money and keeps disappearing. A parent who has never once apologized and never will. A friend whose same choices bring the same wreckage every year. Those who love them hope, then plead, then argue, then bargain, then hope again. Some have tried everything they know, and the hardest part is the slow suspicion that nothing they do will make the difference.

Scripture is honest that people can refuse to turn, and that love does not change that. Jesus loved the rich man and watched him walk away. He longed to gather Jerusalem's children and they were unwilling. Through Hosea God speaks of calling Israel and watching it run the farther. The Bible does not tell these stories as failures of the one who loved. Ezekiel goes further and forbids blaming another person for someone's own ways: each answers to God for themselves. That is hard news for those of us who believe that if we just found the right words, the right patience, the right amount of help, the other person would change. Under that belief there is often love, and sometimes something more like control, or a fear of facing what we cannot fix.

So the Bible's wisdom is to keep loving while giving up the role only God can play. Tell the truth about the pattern, as Jesus says to rebuke before he says to forgive. Forgive in the sense Scripture means, letting go of revenge, without pretending the wrong is right and without trusting again what has not been shown to be trustworthy. Words alone do not make it safe to stay. Stop paying for what keeps them from turning, and let them carry their own load. Find people of your own to lean on, a church, a pastor, a counselor, a group for families of those caught in addiction, so that your whole life does not orbit their choices. Pray for them by name. Grieve, as Samuel grieved, and then take the next step God gives you, which may be in a different direction.

The hope Scripture gives is that God is more patient than we are and more able. He is not slow, Peter says, but patient, wanting everyone to come to repentance, and the son in the far country came to his senses when nothing else was left. The vinedresser asked for one more year and dug around the roots. You cannot turn another person's heart, but God can, and he has not stopped loving the one you are waiting for, or you. Some of the people we wait for will come home in this life. Some will not, and the Bible does not promise otherwise. Either way, the love you gave was not wasted, and you are not responsible for the choice that was theirs.
deep.sit: What have you been trying to do for this person that only God can do, and what would it look like to hand that back to him this week?

prayer.lead: A prayer from the depths by someone still waiting when the psalm ends. The site's plain note says it does not promise when the morning comes; it promises that it will, because God's love keeps its word.
prayer.text: I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope. My soul waits for the Lord more than watchmen wait for the morning— more than watchmen wait for the morning.

careLines.text: Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.
Keeping a record of what someone has done to you, for your safety or to get help or justice, is not a failure of love.
A person can forgive and still stay safe, still tell the truth, and still ask for justice.
Words alone do not make it safe to stay.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
